surveyDefinition.title: Skin Care Products — consumer survey (U.S.)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on skincare routines, purchase drivers, and sensitivity to efficacy claims.

segments.name: Routine Minimalists
segments.description: Use only 1-2 basic products (cleanser, moisturizer) with no targeted concerns; buy on autopilot, price-sensitive, low engagement with claims.

segments.name: Efficacy Buyers
segments.description: Have specific skin concerns (aging, hyperpigmentation, acne) and actively research clinically proven ingredients; willing to pay more for visible results.

segments.name: Sensorial Luxury Buyers
segments.description: High engagement with premium textures, fragrances, and packaging; low price sensitivity; purchase as a treat or self-care ritual.

segments.name: Clean-Conscious Shoppers
segments.description: Prioritize natural, sustainable, and non-toxic formulations; willing to trade some efficacy for clean ingredients; sensitive to greenwashing.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Skin Care Products buyers in U.S.. It asks how people use Skin Care Products, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in U.S. who buy or use Skin Care Products for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who have purchased at least one skin care product for personal use in the past 12 months; Primary decision-maker for their own skin care purchases; Ages 18 and older. Excluded: Professional buyers (e.g., dermatology clinics, spas, salons) purchasing for resale or professional use; Individuals purchasing solely as gifts for others; Children under 18.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy skin care products for personal use, pay for them out of pocket at retail or online, and make the purchase decision themselves. While some professional products are sold to salons, the dominant consumer market is direct-to-consumer, so this is a pure B2C segment.
respondentBehaviours: Regularly purchases skin care products (e.g., cleansers, moisturizers, serums, sunscreens)
Researches products online, reads reviews, follows influencers or dermatologist recommendations
May have specific skin concerns (acne, aging, sensitivity, hyperpigmentation)
Brand loyal but open to switching for better efficacy or price
Purchases through multiple channels: drugstores, department stores, specialty beauty retailers, e-commerce, subscription boxes
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by mapping the respondent's current skincare routine — which products they use, how many steps, and how often — and their primary skin concerns. It then moves into the purchase journey, covering what triggers a buy, where they learn and shop, and what ultimately decides the choice, including spend. Next, it explores their preferences and expectations: must-have attributes, quality cues, the weight of clean or clinical claims, and the trade-offs they are willing to make. It closes with satisfaction, unmet needs, and switching triggers, revealing where the market is heading for…

metadata.segmentation_lens: Combination of usage/behavioural and jobs-to-be-done: the axis that separates buyers is the depth and purpose of their skincare routine — from minimal, functional use to multi-step, outcome-driven regimens. segments.name: Routine Minimalists
segments.description: Use only 1-2 basic products (cleanser, moisturizer) with no targeted concerns; buy on autopilot, price-sensitive, low engagement with claims.
segments.hypothesis: They will report low routine complexity, low spend, and high sensitivity to price promotions.

segments.name: Efficacy Buyers
segments.description: Have specific skin concerns (aging, hyperpigmentation, acne) and actively research clinically proven ingredients; willing to pay more for visible results.
segments.hypothesis: They will prioritize clinical evidence and ingredient lists over brand or price, and will switch brands for better efficacy.

segments.name: Sensorial Luxury Buyers
segments.description: High engagement with premium textures, fragrances, and packaging; low price sensitivity; purchase as a treat or self-care ritual.
segments.hypothesis: They will rate texture and sensory experience as top drivers and show high spend per product.

segments.name: Clean-Conscious Shoppers
segments.description: Prioritize natural, sustainable, and non-toxic formulations; willing to trade some efficacy for clean ingredients; sensitive to greenwashing.
segments.hypothesis: They will value clean claims and sustainable packaging over clinical evidence, and will avoid brands with harsh chemicals.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question 'sf6' (which of these would most likely make you switch) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it forces a single priority choice that cleanly separates the four segments' core motivations.
notes: Routine minimalists are identified by low product count, price sensitivity, and autopilot repurchase.
Efficacy seekers are identified by specific concerns, clinical proof, and willingness to pay for results.
Sensorial luxury buyers are identified by texture/fragrance/packaging priorities and higher spend.
Clean-conscious shoppers are identified by natural/sustainable ingredient priorities and green packaging preferences.
16 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by mapping the respondent's current skincare routine — which products they use, how many steps, and how often — and their primary skin concerns. It then moves into the purchase journey, covering what triggers a buy, where they learn and shop, and what ultimately decides the choice, including spend. Next, it explores their preferences and expectations: must-have attributes, quality cues, the weight of clean or clinical claims, and the trade-offs they are willing to make. It closes with satisfaction, unmet needs, and switching triggers, revealing where the market is heading for…
storyline_notes: Added a 'routine complexity' beat in consumer_profile to capture the depth of engagement, which is central to separating minimalists from efficacy seekers.
Moved 'skin concerns' earlier in consumer_profile because they drive the jobs-to-be-done lens.
In buying_behavior, placed 'decision drivers' before 'spend' to build from attitudinal to sensitive financial questions.
In preferences_expectations, added 'claims and credentials' as a distinct beat to separate clean-conscious shoppers from clinical efficacy seekers.
In satisfaction_future_intent, merged advocacy into overall satisfaction to keep the section focused on unmet needs and switching.
All beats are answerable with closed questions and avoid demographics, income, or geography.
metadata.classification_reason: Everyday consumers buy skin care products for personal use, pay for them out of pocket at retail or online, and make the purchase decision themselves. While some professional products are sold to salons, the dominant consumer market is direct-to-consumer, so this is a pure B2C segment.
